About: Forced Oscillation — the Frequency That Gets an Answer

Source

Topic
Mechanics — forced & damped oscillations
Concept
The amplitude peaks BELOW the natural frequency and slides further below it as damping rises — but the phase passes through 90° AT the natural frequency, for every damping.
Audience
JEE / NCERT Class 11–12
Misconception targeted
“Resonance is when you drive at the natural frequency, and that is where the amplitude peaks.” Those are two different frequencies.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The driven oscillator

A mass m on a spring has natural angular frequency ω₀ and damping α, and a hand drives it with a force F(t) = F₀ cos Ωt at a driving frequency Ω. Once the start-up transient has died away the mass oscillates at Ω, with a steady amplitude A and a phase lag φ behind the force — that steady motion is what is drawn here. Driving at every Ω in turn, where will A be largest?

2 · The peak of A(Ω)

Damping is low, α = 0.5 rad/s, and ω₀ = 10 rad/s.

3 · The mass against the force

The drive is moved to far below ω₀, then to far above it. How does the mass's motion compare with the driving force in the two cases?

4 · Lowering the damping

ω₀ is held at 10 rad/s and the damping α is lowered from 0.5 to 0.2 rad/s. What happens to the peak of the A(Ω) curve?

5 · Driving exactly at ω₀

The drive is set to Ω = ω₀ exactly, and the damping is then swept across its whole range. What does the phase lag φ read?

Forced Oscillation

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A hand pushes a mass on a spring back and forth at a frequency Ω that you choose. The sim shows the size of the steady swing, and how far it lags the push, at every Ω.

What you'll learn

  • How the steady amplitude A depends on the driving frequency Ω, the natural frequency ω₀ and the damping α.
  • How the mass moves relative to the driving force as Ω changes.
  • How to read the resonance peak and the phase lag off the sim.
A hand drives a mass on a spring. The sim shows the steady motion, after the start-up has died away.

What's on screen

  • Hand: the driven end and its force arrow F(t). Its small swing marks the phase of the push. It is not drawn to scale.
  • Mass: the blue box. A two-trace scope beside it shows the hand and the mass over the last few cycles.
  • Amplitude curve: the steady amplitude A against Ω, with an amber marker at your Ω.
  • Two vertical lines on the curve: a solid one at the peak, ω_res, and a dashed one at ω₀.
See itDrive the mass at the opening settings. Watch for: the amber hand bar and the blue mass moving up and down together on the left.

03

The steady motion has a fixed amplitude and phase lag

With the force F₀ cos Ωt, the start-up motion dies away as e−αt. What remains moves at the driving frequency Ω, lagging the force by φ:

x = A cos(Ωt − φ)
The sim draws only this steady motion.
A = F₀ / ( m √((ω₀² − Ω²)² + 4α²Ω²) )
tan φ = 2αΩ / (ω₀² − Ω²)
Amplitude and lag, with φ between 0° and 180°.
  • Ω far below ω₀: the spring wins. A ≈ F₀/(mω₀²) and φ ≈ 0°, so the mass moves with the force. At Ω = 1 rad/s, φ = 0.6°.
  • Ω far above ω₀: the mass's inertia wins, and φ nears 180°, so the mass moves against the force. At Ω = 18 rad/s, φ = 175°.
See itDrive at Ω = 18 rad/s, above ω₀. Watch for: the two scope traces moving in opposite directions, with φ near 175°.
04

The amplitude peaks a little below ω₀

A is largest where the square root in its denominator is smallest. That happens at ω_res, not at ω₀:

ω_res = √(ω₀² − 2α²)
The solid line on the curve. It exists only for α < ω₀/√2.
  • At ω₀ = 10 and α = 0.50, ω_res = 9.975 rad/s. The peak is only 0.025 rad/s below ω₀, so the two lines almost touch.
  • More damping pushes the peak lower: ω_res = 9.59 rad/s at α = 2, and 7.07 rad/s at α = 5.
  • For ω₀ = 10, any α from 7.07 rad/s up gives no peak. The curve then falls steadily from its value at Ω = 0, F₀/(mω₀²) = 0.010 m.
See itSet α = 5 and drive at the peak, Ω = 7.05 rad/s. Watch for: the solid peak line left of the dashed ω₀ line, and the readout ω_res = 7.071 rad/s.
05

At Ω = ω₀ the lag is exactly 90° for every damping

At Ω = ω₀ the term ω₀² − Ω² is zero, so tan φ = 2αΩ/0 and φ = 90°, whatever α is.

  • Force and velocity are then in step. The hand pushes the mass the way it is already moving, so it adds energy at the greatest rate.
  • The lag climbs from near 0° to near 180° as Ω crosses ω₀. Light damping makes the climb steep. At Ω = 9 and 11 rad/s the lag is 25° and 152° for α = 0.50, and 11° and 168° for α = 0.20.
  • The amplitude at Ω = ω₀ is F₀/(2mαω₀). That is 0.100 m at α = 0.50 and 0.250 m at α = 0.20.

The amplitude peak moves as α changes. The 90° crossing at ω₀ does not.

See itDrive at Ω = ω₀ with heavy damping, α = 2. Watch for: φ = 90.0°, with the mass crossing equilibrium as the force peaks.
06

Less damping makes a taller, narrower peak

  • Height. The peak is F₀/(2mα√(ω₀² − α²)), about F₀/(2mαω₀) for light damping. It grows as 1/α.
  • Against the static value. The sim's "× static" label reads 10× at α = 0.50, 25× at α = 0.20 and 100× at α = 0.05, for ω₀ = 10.
  • Width. The amplitude stays above 0.71 of the peak over a band about 2α wide. That is 1.0 rad/s at α = 0.50, and 0.4 rad/s at α = 0.20.
  • Position. ω_res moves toward ω₀ as α falls, but only reaches it at α = 0.

A lightly damped system answers strongly in a narrow band of Ω. A heavily damped one answers weakly and in a wide band.

See itLower α to 0.20 and drive at Ω = 10 rad/s. Watch for: the peak label reading 25× static, and A = 0.2500 m.
07

Where it matters

  • A child on a swing. Pushing once per swing, in step with the motion, adds energy every cycle. Small pushes then build a large swing.
  • Radio tuners. A tuning circuit obeys the same kind of equation. It answers strongly in a narrow band of frequencies, so one station is picked out. Low damping makes the band narrow.
  • Buildings in earthquakes. A building responds most when the ground shakes near its own natural frequency. Tall towers can carry a heavy damped mass that absorbs some of that motion.
08

Summary

In one line. A driven mass settles into steady motion at the driving frequency. This sim lets you vary Ω, ω₀ and α, and read the amplitude and lag.

Key points

  • The steady motion is x = A cos(Ωt − φ), with A and φ set by Ω, ω₀ and α.
  • The amplitude peaks at ω_res = √(ω₀² − 2α²), a little below ω₀.
  • The lag is 90° at Ω = ω₀ for every α.
  • Less damping gives a taller and narrower peak.

Common mix-ups

  • "The amplitude peaks at ω₀." It peaks at ω_res, a little below. Only the 90° lag is exactly at ω₀.
  • "The mass always moves with the force." That holds only well below ω₀. Well above ω₀ it moves against the force.
  • "Every damped system has a resonance peak." With α ≥ ω₀/√2 the curve has no peak.

Things to try on your own

  • Set Ω = ω₀, then slide α from 0.05 to 9 and watch φ while A falls.
  • Set α = 1 and move ω₀ to 6 and 14. Compare where the solid and dashed lines sit.
